result: The study demonstrates that an optogenetic neural replacement strategy using ChR2+ motor neurons with H57-597 mAb immunosuppression can effectively restore innervation of severely affected skeletal muscles in the SOD1G93A mouse model of ALS. Engrafted motor neurons were present in all treated mice (n>84), showed significant axonal projection and robust muscle fiber reinnervation, even when engrafted after symptom onset and maintained until late-stage disease.
evaluation: All three reviewers explicitly affirm this core finding. Reviewer 1 states it is "convincing that embryonic stem cell derived motor neurons can be transplanted into and applied to reinnervate the muscles in an ALS mouse model." Reviewer 3 confirms "convincing evidence that optogenetic stimulation of ChR2-expressing motor neurons implanted in muscles effectively restore innervation." Reviewer 2 acknowledges the manuscript "addresses some of the challenges that will need to be overcome, such as immune rejection of the allograft."

result: Daily optical stimulation training (OST) resulted in a 9.4-fold increase in maximal tetanic force compared to untrained mice, with trained mice achieving up to 22.7% of total residual muscle force (representing a >13-fold improvement). OST reinforced connectivity between engrafted motor neurons and muscle fibers and prevented atrophy of reinnervated muscle fibers.
evaluation: Reviewers do not question these quantitative findings about OST effects. Reviewer 3 explicitly states the data "supported by convincing data presented in the paper" regarding the method's ability to "selectively control the function of implicated muscles." The physiological improvements from training are accepted as demonstrated by the experimental data.

result: FK506 immunosuppression enabled graft survival at the graft site in all animals but caused three major problems: complete prevention of muscle fiber reinnervation, intraneural tumor formation in most mice, and body mass decline in 44.4% of SOD1G93A mice. FK506 also caused significant axon loss in tibial and common peroneal nerves in both wild-type and SOD1G93A mice.
evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge these findings about FK506's adverse effects. The data on FK506's problems are presented as factual observations that led to testing alternative immunosuppression approaches. These findings are implicitly accepted as they provide the rationale for the H57-597 mAb approach that reviewers explicitly support.

result: H57-597 mAb treatment does not significantly alter axon size distribution or counts compared to untreated SOD1G93A mice and was well tolerated during transient administration from symptom-onset to late-stage disease, avoiding the adverse effects observed with FK506.
evaluation: Reviewers accept this finding as part of the overall demonstration of successful immunosuppression strategy. Reviewer 2 notes the manuscript "addresses some of the challenges that will need to be overcome, such as immune rejection of the allograft," implicitly accepting the H57-597 solution. No concerns are raised about the safety or efficacy claims for this immunosuppressant.

result: Only 10.5% of endplates were innervated by engrafted ChR2+ motor neurons in untrained mice, but these reinnervated endplates were functional as acute optical nerve stimulation induced positive contractile responses in all late-stage SOD1G93A mice tested. Motor neuron subtype identity did not significantly affect the amplitude of muscle response to acute optical stimulation.
evaluation: Reviewers do not question these quantitative findings about innervation levels and functional responses. The demonstration of functional reinnervation is central to the reviewers' positive assessment. Reviewer 3 confirms the evidence shows motor neurons "effectively restore innervation," which encompasses these functional measurements.

result: Repetitive optical nerve stimulation (ONS) pulses did not induce rapid muscle fatigue, whereas equivalent electrical nerve stimulation (ENS) pulses did result in rapid muscle fatigue.
evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge this comparative finding about ONS versus ENS. This advantage of the optogenetic approach is implicitly accepted as part of the overall demonstration that the method can "selectively control the function of targeted muscles" (Reviewer 3), which includes avoiding fatigue.

result: The average cross-sectional area (CSA) of muscle fibers innervated by engrafted ChR2+ motor neurons was similar to fibers innervated by residual endogenous motor neurons (922.3 vs 1018.3 μm²) and significantly greater than denervated fibers (525.4 μm²), demonstrating prevention of atrophy in reinnervated fibers.
evaluation: Reviewers do not question these histological measurements supporting atrophy prevention. The dCALMS analysis data are presented as supporting evidence for the OST benefits, and reviewers accept the overall conclusion that the approach prevents muscle atrophy, as evidenced by their positive assessment of the therapeutic strategy.

result: Without immunosuppression, graft survival was extremely low (<5%) at 35 days post-engraftment in SOD1G93A mice. However, in rare surviving cases, robust intramuscular axon growth and partial NMJ reinnervation were observed, with optical stimulation inducing weak tetanic contractions. Poor survival was attributed to host-vs-graft rejection rather than disease-related toxicity.
evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge these initial findings that established the need for immunosuppression. These observations are accepted as the foundation for developing the immunosuppression strategy that reviewers explicitly support. The interpretation that rejection rather than toxicity caused graft loss is implicitly accepted through reviewers' endorsement of the immunosuppression solution.

result: Motor neuron subtype identity appears redundant for innervating mixed fiber type muscles in SOD1G93A mice, suggesting a single motor neuron type produced at scale could potentially target multiple different muscles in each patient.
evaluation: Reviewers do not question this finding or its translational implication. The observation that motor neuron subtype doesn't affect innervation success is accepted as part of the overall demonstration of the approach's feasibility and is consistent with reviewers' positive assessment of the therapeutic potential.

result: The authors propose that this combinatorial strategy (allogeneic cells, immunosuppression, optical stimulation) could be universally compatible with ALS patients, target multiple muscles independently, integrate with brain-computer interfaces to restore autologous movement control, and have broad utility for other neurogenic causes of paralysis including spinal cord injury and stroke.
evaluation: Reviewers acknowledge the therapeutic potential but do not explicitly endorse these specific translational claims. Reviewer 1 states the work "will be of broad interest to researchers and medical biologists to develop new strategies," suggesting future development rather than confirmed applicability. Reviewer 2 notes "challenges that will need to be overcome," indicating uncertainty about clinical translation. These are speculative extrapolations from the mouse data that reviewers treat cautiously.

result: The authors acknowledge that further investigation is required to confirm the strategy in alternate ALS models with longer lifespans, that maintenance therapy may be needed for long-term graft survival, that demonstrating efficacy with human motor neurons is the biggest challenge, and that scaling up in larger animal models is necessary.
evaluation: Reviewers implicitly support these acknowledgments of limitations. Reviewer 2 explicitly notes the manuscript addresses "challenges that will need to be overcome," aligning with the authors' recognition of remaining hurdles. These statements of future research needs are consistent with reviewers' cautious optimism about clinical translation.
